passage: Siddharth knew which stories made people lean in. In the hostel common room, he mentioned that Arun had failed the maths test, with a shrug, as if he pitied him, and three boys laughed and made room for him on the sofa. It worked again the next week. He was invited to the football group chat and everyone knew his name. But Pradeep, his roommate, went quiet. One night Pradeep said, "I stopped telling you things. I saw what happened to Arun's story." Siddharth lay awake. He had a full sofa and nobody he could talk to. On Saturday he told Arun he was sorry, and joined the football trials on his own merit, instead of by telling stories.

qa.q: What did Siddharth mention about Arun in the common room?
qa.a: That Arun had failed the maths test.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth lie awake after Pradeep spoke?
qa.a: He realised his gossip had won him a place on the sofa but had cost him trust; he felt hollow, with a full sofa and nobody he could talk to.

qa.q: What could Siddharth do to belong in an honest way?
qa.a: Apologise to those he hurt, as he did with Arun, and find belonging through real interests like the football trials rather than gossip and charm.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see Siddharth's habit?
qa.a: As a reason not to trust Siddharth. Pradeep said they stopped telling Siddharth things after seeing what happened to Arun's story, so Pradeep is protecting themself.

grounding: The protagonist climbs the social ladder with charm and gossip, feels hollow and chooses honest ways to belong.

passage:
Friday
I'm finally in. Last year nobody in the "back bench group" knew my name. Now I sit right in the middle of it.
Here's how. I figured out what they wanted: news. So I gave it to them. Who liked whom, whose parents were fighting, what the teacher said in the staff room. I laughed at the right jokes. I told everyone what they wanted to hear.
Tonight Anirban messaged me. "Did you tell them about my dad's job? I told only you." I didn't reply. I did tell them. It got me a laugh and a seat.
I thought I'd feel great, being popular. Instead I feel hollow. They like my gossip, not me. And the one person who actually trusted me, I traded away.
Tomorrow I'm going to call Anirban and say sorry, no excuses. And I'm going to stop trading stories. If they only want me for news, then they don't really want me.
Sahil

qa.q: What did Anirban tell only Sahil?
How does Sahil feel now that the group accepts Sahil?
qa.a: Sahil feels hollow and guilty, knowing they like the gossip, not the person, and that a friend's trust was betrayed.

qa.q: What is Sahil planning to do, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Sahil plans to apologise to Anirban without excuses and stop trading gossip, choosing honest ways to belong instead.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel on learning the secret was shared?
qa.a: Anirban probably feels betrayed and hurt, having trusted only Sahil with it.

grounding: A teen who used charm and gossip to climb socially feels hollow, sees the cost to trust and chooses honest belonging.
